result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full paper proposes AgentCF, which uses LLM-powered user agents to simulate user-item interactions in recommender systems, including autonomous item selection/click-like behavior and ranking evaluation on recommendation datasets.
inclusion_criteria_triggered: Uses LLM-powered agents as simulated user agents/user response models
Applies the agents to recommender-system simulation of user-item interactions
Evaluates item recommendation/ranking settings with candidate item ranking and NDCG metrics

categories.evidence: Experiments use Amazon review datasets, specifically “CDs and Vinyl” and “Office Products,” for item recommendation/ranking.
categories.reviewer_notes: The datasets span multiple Amazon product categories; coded as e_commerce because the setting is product recommendation from Amazon reviews.

categories.evidence: The paper explicitly analyzes “position bias” and “popularity bias” in candidate ranking and states that it introduces popular bias and position bias in candidate selection.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper uses the terms position bias and popularity bias, which are not exact taxonomy labels. Position bias was mapped to measurement_bias and popularity bias to historical_bias conservatively.

categories.evidence: User agents and item agents are implemented with LLMs; the paper describes “LLM-powered agents,” uses text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo, and prompts agents for autonomous item selection and reflection.
categories.reviewer_notes: Prompt procedures structure the interaction, but user behaviour is generated by the LLM rather than fixed if-then rules.

categories.evidence: The method uses real user behavioural sequences/interaction records as training data and prompts LLM agents to update user self-introductions/preferences through collaborative reflection.
categories.reviewer_notes: Initial user memory is generic, but personalized user representations are updated from historical interaction logs using LLM-generated memory text.

categories.evidence: The user agent includes short-term and long-term memory modules and a reflection mechanism to revise preferences and decisions after interactions.
categories.reviewer_notes: No personality theory or affective state model is reported; memory and reflection support cognition-inspired coding.

categories.evidence: Agents autonomously select between candidate items; update memories after feedback from real interaction records; and the paper simulates user-user, item-item, and collective interactions.
categories.reviewer_notes: Proactiveness was not coded because agents appear to respond to given interaction/ranking tasks rather than deciding independently when to engage with the system.

categories.evidence: User agents have self-introductions/preference descriptions, choose items from candidates, use short-term and long-term memory, and perform collaborative reflection to update memory.
categories.reviewer_notes: Planning was not reported as a module; the paper contrasts its approach with planning-based agents but does not implement explicit planning for the user agent.

categories.evidence: Feedback is implemented by collaborative reflection over disparities between agent decisions and real-world records, and by mutual memory updates between user and item agents through interactions.
categories.reviewer_notes: Retraining was not coded because the LLM is fixed and the paper states there is no gradient-based learning; updates are memory-based.

categories.evidence: User short-term and long-term memories are updated over interaction steps; item memory is also updated with adopter preferences and propagated to later interactions.
categories.reviewer_notes: No ML model feedback loop was coded because simulated interactions are not used to retrain an ML recommender. Feature feedback is coded because user and item memory/features are updated through interaction feedback.

categories.evidence: The paper evaluates recommendation/ranking performance with NDCG@1, NDCG@5, and NDCG@10 and compares against BPR, SASRec, Pop, BM25, and LLMRank.
categories.reviewer_notes: Bias analyses are reported, but the main recommender evaluation uses standard accuracy/performance metrics; no explicit scalability evaluation is provided.

categories.evidence: The simulator is evaluated by comparing agent choices/rankings against held-out real user interaction records from Amazon review datasets, including proportions of correct choices and NDCG metrics.
categories.reviewer_notes: No live user study or online user testing is reported. Scalability is discussed as a limitation due to API costs, not evaluated.

result.paper_level_notes: Full text confirms that AgentCF is directly relevant: it simulates user-item interactions in recommender systems using LLM-powered user and item agents, with collaborative reflection and memory updates based on real interaction logs.

categories.evidence: The agent architecture includes memory retrieval, memory writing, and memory reflection inspired by human cognitive processes. Profiles include social traits described as activity, conformity, and diversity. Emotional memories record feelings, fatigue, and satisfaction and drive exit/evaluation actions.
categories.reviewer_notes: Personality_aware is based on the paper's claim that social traits capture elements of personality and characteristics in recommendation scenarios, not on a standard Big Five model.

categories.evidence: Agents independently decide whether to watch, rate, ignore, proceed to the next page, or exit. Their decisions depend on current recommendations, user profile, factual/emotional memory, satisfaction, and fatigue. Agents can decide to exit the recommender system.
categories.reviewer_notes: Social_ability is not selected because the paper does not implement agent-to-agent or user-to-user social interaction, despite using 'social traits'.

categories.evidence: Agent4Rec agents have profile, memory, and action modules. The memory module includes factual and emotional memories, and the paper introduces an emotion-driven memory reflection mechanism where agents introspect satisfaction and fatigue.
categories.reviewer_notes: Planning is not selected because no explicit planning module or multi-step goal planning is described.

categories.evidence: Agents use emotion-driven self-reflection over prior interactions. categories.reviewer_notes: No agent-to-agent feedback loop is implemented.

categories.evidence: Individual agents update emotional memory and reflect on satisfaction/fatigue over interactions. Simulated interactions are inserted into recommender training data for retraining. The filter-bubble experiment describes recommendation exposure leading to more views, which are then introduced into new training data and influence subsequent exposure.
categories.reviewer_notes: Feature_feedback_loop and sampling_feedback_loop are not selected because the paper does not clearly model changes in observable user features or population composition.

categories.evidence: Recommendation strategies are evaluated using metrics such as average viewing ratio, number/ratio of likes, exit page, satisfaction score, Recall@20, and NDCG@20. The filter-bubble experiment evaluates content diversity using genre diversity and top-1 genre proportion.
categories.reviewer_notes: Scalability is not selected because the paper reports simulation scale but does not evaluate computational cost, runtime, throughput, or deployment feasibility.

categories.evidence: Agent alignment is evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1, rating-distribution comparison, social-trait distributions, ablations, and statistical tests. Simulated behaviour is compared with MovieLens-1M and other offline datasets such as Steam and Amazon-Book.
categories.reviewer_notes: No real-world user testing is reported. Scalability is not selected because the paper does not evaluate simulator runtime or computational scaling, despite using 1,000 agents.

result.paper_level_notes: The paper is a strong inclusion: it directly proposes and evaluates an LLM-based generative-agent user simulator for recommender-system simulation. Main limitations reported by the authors include datasource constraints, limited action space, and LLM hallucination.

result.title: TRACE: A Scalable and Extensible Framework for Auditing YouTube's Recommendation Algorithm
result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full paper proposes TRACE, an LLM-driven persona-based user-agent framework for simulating user journeys through YouTube recommendations. Agents choose recommended videos and generate interaction traces for auditing recommendation dynamics.
inclusion_criteria_triggered: Uses an LLM as a simulated user agent/user response model: personas are continuous inputs to an LLM that makes decisions on behalf of agents.
Used in recommender-system simulation/auditing: TRACE audits YouTube's recommendation algorithm through simulated user journeys.
Involves item recommendation: agents scrape visible YouTube video recommendations and select videos to watch.

categories.evidence: The framework audits YouTube's recommendation algorithm, and agents select among visible recommended videos.
categories.reviewer_notes: YouTube is a video recommendation setting.

categories.evidence: The paper discusses algorithmic bias, potential filter bubbles, ideological trajectories, and an 'initial recommendation bias', but it does not classify these as representation, measurement, historical, or evaluation bias.
categories.reviewer_notes: Bias is discussed, but not using the taxonomy's specific bias categories.

categories.evidence: TRACE uses LLM-driven personas for decisions; agents follow a two-phase loop with predefined warm-up videos; the paper states individual LLM decisions are stochastic and that mixed mode probabilistically selects from a weighted persona pool.
categories.reviewer_notes: Predefined rules refer to the fixed experimental loop and warm-up/context procedure, not a fully rule-based user model.

categories.evidence: Personas are described as detailed natural-language descriptions of interests, biases, and viewing habits, and the proof of concept defines Pro-Israel, Pro-Palestine, and Neutral personas, but the construction basis/source of these personas is not specified as logs, random sampling, or LLM generation.
categories.reviewer_notes: Personas appear researcher-defined; no allowed label directly captures manually specified personas.

categories.evidence: The paper frames TRACE as simulating 'psychologically plausible user behavior' and includes an LLM decision-making step where the agent chooses among recommendations based on persona interests and viewing habits.
categories.reviewer_notes: No explicit personality theory such as Big Five is used; 'persona' alone was not coded as personality-aware.

categories.evidence: The LLM makes decisions on behalf of the agent, selecting videos from scraped recommendations; agent choices depend on the current YouTube recommendation page during iterative navigation.
categories.reviewer_notes: Proactiveness was not coded because the agent appears to operate for a configured number of steps and selects from presented recommendations rather than deciding when to initiate or stop interaction.

categories.evidence: TRACE uses explicit personas as user profiles, and agents perform actions such as selecting recommended videos, navigating to them, and simulating viewing events.
categories.reviewer_notes: Memory was not coded because the paper reports database logging and YouTube personalization but does not clearly state that the LLM agent uses an internal memory module.

categories.evidence: The simulation iterates through recommendations and watch events to study evolving recommendation pathways, but the paper does not implement self-reflection, agent-to-agent interaction, or retraining, and the internal YouTube feedback mechanism is black-box.
categories.reviewer_notes: There is an interaction loop with YouTube, but it does not fit the available implementation labels cleanly.

categories.evidence: Agents select videos from YouTube recommendations, simulate watch events, and then receive subsequent recommendations, allowing recommendation pathways and ideological lean scores to evolve over time.
categories.reviewer_notes: Coded conservatively as outcome feedback because recommendations affect simulated viewing outcomes that shape later recommendation exposure; no user preference updating or model retraining is reported.

categories.evidence: The proof of concept computes a rank-weighted lean metric to quantify ideological orientation of recommendation lists and analyzes polarization/filter-bubble dynamics rather than accuracy.
categories.reviewer_notes: Scalability evidence mainly concerns TRACE as an auditing framework, not YouTube as the recommender system.

categories.evidence: The proof of concept reports stance-coherent choices for personas and demonstrates scale/cost characteristics: 100 agents per persona, 50-step sequences, less than $0.01 per agent for Mistral Small, $0.10 per agent proxies, and 10 concurrent instances on commodity hardware.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper states the proof of concept is methodological and does not validate simulated behavior against real users or offline user logs.

result.paper_level_notes: Full text confirms the abstract-only inclusion. TRACE is primarily an auditing/simulation framework for YouTube recommendations using LLM-driven persona agents, with a proof-of-concept ideological recommendation audit.

categories.reviewer_notes: Other covers relation/network, stance modelling, and agent training modules. Self_reflection was not selected because reflection is not described as an explicit agent module.

categories.reviewer_notes: Retraining is interpreted as model updating of the intervention policy, not retraining the LLM user agents during the simulation.

categories.evidence: Agents update memory and stance over rounds; the contextual bandit policy is updated from simulated rewards; platform outcomes such as cross-viewpoint interaction, toxicity, and misinformation feed back into policy optimization; user context embeddings incorporate recent memory and network message passing.

categories.evidence: The intervention/recommender policy is evaluated on objectives such as cross-stance interaction, toxicity reduction, stance diversity, and misinformation propagation ratio.

result.paper_level_notes: The paper is primarily framed as social-platform intervention and policy simulation, but the recommender-system component is concrete: a recommender system selects user-post pairs and LLM agents generate user reactions. categories.value: profile; action; memory; planning; self_reflection; other
categories.evidence: The paper describes persona/profile, perception, memory, and brain/action modules; the brain translates evidence into action plans; post-interaction reflection synthesizes memories and feeds them back into episodic memory.
categories.reviewer_notes: Other refers primarily to the perception module for visual thumbnail captions and multimodal cues. Planning is coded because the brain module explicitly generates action plans and uses multi-step reasoning/refinement.

categories.reviewer_notes: The paper uses SimUSER outputs to refine recommender parameters, but it does not clearly describe retraining an ML model with simulated interaction data, so retraining was not selected.

categories.evidence: Each agent updates episodic and knowledge-graph memory with watched/rated items and reflections, allowing future decisions to depend on prior interactions.
categories.reviewer_notes: The implemented loop is at the individual simulated-user level. Broader recommender retraining or population-composition loops are not clearly implemented.

result.paper_level_notes: This is a strong inclusion. It directly proposes LLM-based simulated users for item recommender-system evaluation, with persona, memory, perception, action, and reflection mechanisms.

categories.evidence: The study collects simulated and human conversations for comparison; it does not report self-reflection updates, agent-to-agent interaction, or retraining based on simulated feedback.

result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full text clearly uses an RL-trained LLM agent to simulate personalized step-wise online shopping behavior and predict next actions/clicks. This triggers exclusion for general user/human behavior simulation outside a recommender-system context.

Partial relevance to Inclusion 3: evaluates next-action and click/action prediction in online shopping, but not within a recommender-system setting.

categories.reviewer_notes: Although excluded as not a recommender-system simulation, the application domain is clearly e-commerce/online shopping.

categories.evidence: The paper discusses performance issues such as over-selecting frequent/simple actions, but does not explicitly address representation, measurement, historical, or evaluation bias.

categories.evidence: The framework uses explicit user persona profiles; generates actions such as click/input/terminate; observes behavior history in the session; and generates an intermediate rationale before the action.
categories.reviewer_notes: The 'other' label refers to the rationale/reasoning output. No explicit planning or self-reflection module is reported.

categories.evidence: The paper evaluates next-action simulation from logged sessions and trains the LLM with SFT/RL, but does not describe a simulation feedback loop where simulated interactions update a recommender, agents, or environment over time.

categories.evidence: No individual preference update loop, ML recommender feedback loop, sampling feedback loop, outcome feedback loop, or feature feedback loop is modeled in the simulation.

categories.evidence: The experiments evaluate next-action prediction and simulator behavior; no recommender system or recommendation algorithm is evaluated.
categories.reviewer_notes: This supports the full-text exclusion decision: the paper is not framed as recommender-system simulation.

categories.reviewer_notes: No live user testing is reported. Model size/context ablations are reported, but not runtime, throughput, or deployment scalability evaluation.

result.paper_level_notes: Full text confirms a strong fit for LLM-based personalized user simulation in e-commerce, but not for recommender-system simulation specifically. categories.evidence: The paper frames the LLM as an offline evaluator/world model and explicitly avoids replaying full interaction dynamics; no preference updates, agent-to-agent interaction, or retraining loop is reported.
categories.reviewer_notes: No implemented feedback loop is described.

categories.reviewer_notes: Static offline evaluation only.

categories.reviewer_notes: Although the setting is recommender evaluation, the paper primarily evaluates the simulator/judge, not a recommender system itself.

title: Selecting User Histories to Generate LLM Users for Cold-Start Item Recommendation
pdf_filename: Selecting User Histories to Generate LLM Users for Cold-Start Item Recommendation.pdf

result.title: Selecting User Histories to Generate LLM Users for Cold-Start Item Recommendation
result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full paper explicitly uses an LLM as a simulated user/user response model by prompting it with a user's full interaction history to choose between cold-start items. The generated user preferences are used as simulated interaction data for item recommendation, and the recommender is evaluated using cold-start item recall.
inclusion_criteria_triggered: Uses an LLM as a simulated user/user response model: the paper says it leverages the LLM as a user and prompts it with user histories to generate cold-start item pairwise preferences.
The LLM user is used in a recommender-system simulation/data-augmentation context for cold-start item recommendation.
The setting is item recommendation, evaluated with recall@K/cold recall@K on Amazon Product Review datasets.

categories.evidence: Experiments use the Sports and Beauty categories from the public Amazon Product Reviews datasets, with item recommendation over products.
categories.reviewer_notes: Although two product categories are used, both are e-commerce product recommendation domains.

categories.evidence: The related-work discussion states that LLMs may overemphasize popular content because frequently mentioned items dominate pretraining corpora, disadvantaging less-represented items; the authors say their pairwise cold-start setup mitigates popularity bias.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper explicitly discusses popularity bias/less-represented items, but the taxonomy has no direct popularity-bias label; representation_bias is the closest supported label.

categories.evidence: The simulated user response is generated by an LLM, specifically LLaMa-3.2-3B-Instruct. The method also randomly samples cold-start item pairs and uses probabilistic user selection via a sigmoid policy.
categories.reviewer_notes: Machine-learning modelling is central because the LLM acts as the user and an RL policy selects users. Stochastic modelling is included because random sampling and probabilistic policy selection are part of the simulation/augmentation process.

categories.evidence: The LLM is prompted with each user's entire training interaction history; user features are created from historical item metadata, ratings, and review histories in Amazon Product Review data.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper samples/selects users and item pairs, but the user representation itself is primarily constructed from historical recommender-system logs rather than LLM-generated profiles.

categories.evidence: The user simulation is based on interaction histories, item titles, ratings, and behavioural features; the paper does not model personality traits, affect, cognition, or psychological theory.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper uses terms like 'persona' and 'true preference', but no explicit psychological model or construct is described.

categories.evidence: The LLM independently chooses which of two cold-start items the user would prefer. Its response is conditioned on the presented item pair and the user's interaction history.
categories.reviewer_notes: No evidence of social interaction between agents or proactive decisions about when/how to interact; the LLM only responds to prompts.

categories.evidence: The prompt represents a user through their interaction history, which serves as a user profile/memory. The LLM produces an action-like pairwise preference, treating the chosen item as the positive cold-start item.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper does not describe planning or self-reflection modules. 'Profile' is coded because the historical item list functions as the user representation.

categories.evidence: The generated LLM preference data are added as augmented data, and two-tower recommender models are trained with the original and augmented data. The policy is also updated iteratively using cold-start recall rewards.
categories.reviewer_notes: No self-reflection or agent-to-agent feedback loop is implemented.

categories.evidence: Simulated LLM interactions are inserted into recommender training through an auxiliary BPR loss, creating an ML-model feedback loop. The RL policy iteratively changes which users are selected for augmentation based on reward, affecting the sampled user subset.
categories.reviewer_notes: The ML-model feedback loop is clear. Sampling_feedback_loop is coded because the learned policy changes the selected augmentation population, though this is an experimental augmentation loop rather than a live platform loop.

categories.evidence: The recommender is evaluated using recall@K, cold recall@K, and warm recall@K. The paper also discusses serving efficiency, number of LLM requests, dataset scale, and GPU-hour costs for policy/reward training.
categories.reviewer_notes: Performance evaluation is central. Scalability is included because the paper explicitly frames the method as scalable/serving-efficient and reports computational-resource details, though runtime benchmarking is limited.

categories.evidence: The paper evaluates 'LLM effectiveness as a user' by comparing LLM-user augmentation against an LLM-interaction-history baseline using downstream cold recall metrics. It also discusses reducing LLM inference requests and improving training efficiency via proxy rewards.
categories.reviewer_notes: The simulator is not directly validated against human judgments or matched historical choices; evaluation is mainly indirect through recommender performance on offline datasets.

result.paper_level_notes: The paper is primarily a recommender data-augmentation method, but it clearly contains an LLM-based simulated user response model: the LLM is prompted with user histories and returns pairwise cold-start item preferences used as synthetic interactions.

result.full_text_reasoning_brief: Full text shows CrowdLLM simulates human decisions/ratings using an LLM plus generative models, including Amazon product-rating experiments framed as useful for recommendation systems. exclusion_criteria_triggered: Does not clearly involve item recommendation such as top-k/top-1 recommendation or user click prediction

Includes a product-rating/user-rating case study connected to recommendation systems

categories.evidence: The paper evaluates user-rating generation on Amazon Beauty and Amazon Music/Musical Instruments datasets, and also includes non-recommender domains such as crowdsourcing and voting.
categories.reviewer_notes: Coded as general_purpose_recommender because the recommender-related experiments span multiple product categories rather than one clearly dominant recommender domain.

categories.evidence: The paper states that LLM-based populations may show 'lack of diversity and undetected bias' and proposes profile and belief generators to create 'sufficiently representative' digital populations matching real population diversity.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper discusses bias mainly as population representativeness/diversity, not as formal measurement, historical, or evaluation bias.

categories.reviewer_notes: Mathematical equations are used to specify the model, but the user behaviour implementation is primarily probabilistic and ML-based rather than deterministic symbolic equations.

categories.evidence: Virtual participants are produced by a random profile generator with noise, and product-rating experiments use Amazon Reviews 2023 data containing user reviews/ratings; CrowdLLM is trained on real human response data.
categories.reviewer_notes: No evidence that the LLM itself generates user profiles/personas for CrowdLLM; LLM-generated personas appear only as a baseline prompting strategy.

categories.evidence: The model explicitly represents human decision-making through personalized 'belief bias' generated for each participant and blended with an LLM reference decision.
categories.reviewer_notes: No formal psychological theory, personality model, affect, memory, or attention model is used; coding is based on the paper's explicit belief/decision-making framing.

categories.evidence: Each simulated participant independently produces a decision/rating/vote, and the generated response depends on the task/problem description and the participant profile/belief bias.
categories.reviewer_notes: No agent-to-agent interaction or proactive choice of when/how to interact is described; interactions are assigned tasks rather than self-initiated.

categories.evidence: CrowdLLM includes a profile generator for participant profiles, produces decisions such as ratings/votes/labels, and includes reference generation, belief generation, and a blender module.
categories.reviewer_notes: No memory, planning, or self-reflection module is reported. 'Other' refers to the belief generator/blender architecture.

categories.evidence: Experiments generate simulated decisions and compare them with human data; there is no described loop where simulated interactions update user agents through reflection, agent-to-agent interaction, or retrain a recommender/user model during simulation.
categories.reviewer_notes: CrowdLLM is trained on human data, but this is not a feedback loop using simulated interaction data.

categories.evidence: The paper does not model user-state updates over time, recommender retraining from simulated interactions, changing sampled populations due to system outcomes, or feature/outcome feedback loops.
categories.reviewer_notes: The simulations are largely static response-generation tasks rather than sequential recommender feedback-loop simulations.

categories.evidence: The recommender system itself is not evaluated; product-rating experiments evaluate CrowdLLM's generated rating distributions using MAE, RMSE, cosine similarity, and Wasserstein distance against human ratings.
categories.reviewer_notes: Metrics are simulator/user-response metrics, not recommender-system metrics such as ranking accuracy, top-k performance, or click prediction.

categories.evidence: The simulator is evaluated with MAE, RMSE, cosine similarity, and Wasserstein distance; the paper studies sample efficiency, cost-saving, number of virtual workers, and scalability; it compares generated behaviour with real datasets including Amazon Reviews, crowdsourcing annotations, and voting records.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper uses existing human-response datasets rather than reporting a new live user study; therefore real_world_data_user_testing was not selected.

result.paper_level_notes: Excluded at full-text stage because the recommender-related case study concerns generating product-rating distributions, not simulating a recommender system that recommends items or predicts clicks/top-k choices. result.title: Toward High-Fidelity Multi-Agent Recommendation: An Agentic Design Framework Integrating RecoWorld and LLMs
result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full text proposes a recommender-system simulation framework with a Cognitive User Agent implemented using an LLM, interacting with a RecBole recommender policy in a RecoWorld environment. The setting involves recommendation slates and top-K evaluation on MovieLens.
inclusion_criteria_triggered: Uses/proposes an LLM as a simulated cognitive user agent/user response model
Used in recommender-system simulation with RecoWorld and RecBole
Recommender setting involves item recommendation slates and top-K metrics

categories.evidence: The preliminary benchmark uses the ml-32m / MovieLens dataset with users, items, and interactions.
categories.reviewer_notes: The framework is general-purpose, but the only specific empirical dataset reported is MovieLens, so coded as movie/video.

categories.evidence: The paper does not explicitly discuss representation, measurement, historical, or evaluation bias. It only mentions persona-defined agent biases generally.
categories.reviewer_notes: The word 'biases' appears in relation to persona/context, but no taxonomy bias type is addressed.

categories.evidence: The recommendation process is formalized as a POMDP with transition and observation probability distributions; the user agent is an LLM-driven reasoning agent.
categories.reviewer_notes: Stochastic modelling is coded from the POMDP/probability-distribution formulation; no fixed rule-based user simulator is described.

categories.evidence: The Cognitive User Agent has a persona/context profile integrating demographics, temporal factors, and history, but the paper does not specify how these profiles are constructed.
categories.reviewer_notes: Although MovieLens logs are used for recommender policy benchmarking, the paper does not clearly state that logs construct the LLM user agents.

categories.evidence: The paper describes a 'Cognitive User Agent' with persona, memory, reasoning, perception, latent interests/satisfaction, and a 'Think it through' process.
categories.reviewer_notes: Personas are mentioned, but not personality theory or traits such as Big Five; affect is not clearly modelled beyond satisfaction.

categories.evidence: The LLM evaluates recommendation slates and chooses actions such as clicking, liking, or skipping; it updates internal state and uses interaction history.
categories.reviewer_notes: Proactiveness is possible because agents generate instructions, but the paper does not clearly show user agents deciding when/how to initiate interactions beyond responding to recommendations.

categories.evidence: The architecture includes persona/context profiles, action choices like clicking/liking/skipping, memory/history, reflective instructions, and a reasoning/perception loop.
categories.reviewer_notes: 'Other' refers to the explicit reasoning/perception component, which is not otherwise represented in the allowed labels.

categories.evidence: The framework has a closed-loop interaction among RecoWorld, RecBole, and the LLM user agent; the user agent updates its internal state and generates reflective instructions; pseudo-reward signals are intended for training/refining policies.
categories.reviewer_notes: Some feedback-loop elements are proposed rather than fully evaluated; retraining is coded because training/refinement using pseudo-rewards is explicitly described.

categories.evidence: The user agent updates internal state over interactions; simulated engagement pseudo-rewards guide policy learning; system recommendations affect clicks, dwell time, ratings, retention, and later feedback.
categories.reviewer_notes: Sampling and feature feedback loops are not clearly specified. Long-term retention is an aim, but platform exit/population change is not explicitly implemented.

categories.evidence: The paper benchmarks BPR, ConvNCF, and NeuMF on MovieLens using Recall@K, NDCG@K, and MRR@K.
categories.reviewer_notes: Beyond-accuracy objectives such as diversity and retention are discussed as goals, but not evaluated with reported metrics.

categories.evidence: The reported preliminary results validate RecBole policy performance only; no evaluation of the LLM user simulator against logs, humans, scalability, or simulator-specific metrics is reported.
categories.reviewer_notes: The multi-turn Cognitive User Agent simulation appears to be future/proposed work rather than empirically evaluated in this short paper.

result.paper_level_notes: This is a doctoral consortium/framework paper. It clearly fits the review scope, but many simulator implementation and evaluation details are proposed at a high level rather than fully instantiated or empirically tested.

result.title: SUBER: An RL Environment with Simulated Human Behavior for Recommender Systems
result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full paper proposes SUBER, a recommender-system simulation environment using LLMs as synthetic users/user response models. The LLM rates recommended items in movie and book recommendation settings and is used to train/evaluate RL-based recommenders.
inclusion_criteria_triggered: Uses/proposes/evaluates an LLM as a simulated user agent or user response model
LLM-based user agent is used in recommender-system simulation
Recommender setting involves item recommendation, including movie and book item recommendations

categories.evidence: The framework is presented as a general RL environment for recommender systems and is experimentally validated in both movie and book recommendation settings.
categories.reviewer_notes: Because the experiments span multiple item domains, coded as general_purpose_recommender per rule.

categories.evidence: The paper discusses that offline evaluation occurs in a static and biased environment and proposes SUBER as an evaluation/training environment to avoid direct real-user interaction.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper does not develop a formal bias-mitigation method; evaluation bias is coded because biased offline evaluation is explicitly discussed as a motivation.

categories.evidence: SUBER uses LLMs to simulate users and rate recommendations. Synthetic user attributes are sampled from distributions/lists, and reward perturbation uses Gaussian or greedy noise. Reward shaping is defined with a mathematical equation.
categories.reviewer_notes: Predefined rules are not coded because user responses are primarily generated by the LLM rather than fixed if-then behavioural scripts.

categories.evidence: The paper states that synthetic users are created using Vicuna, with age sampled from the US age distribution and hobbies/professions randomly selected from predefined lists.
categories.reviewer_notes: Item datasets use MovieLens/TMDB and Amazon Books, but real system logs are not used to construct the synthetic user personas.

categories.evidence: The paper describes preferences, hobbies, interaction history, and concept drift, but does not report a psychological theory, personality model, affect model, or explicit cognitive architecture for user modelling.
categories.reviewer_notes: Although the system has a memory module, this appears to be an engineering component rather than an explicitly cognition-inspired psychological model.

categories.evidence: The LLM independently generates ratings for recommended items, and responses are conditioned on the user profile, queried item, and interaction history stored in memory.
categories.reviewer_notes: No agent-to-agent social interaction or proactive initiation of interactions is reported.

categories.evidence: SUBER includes user descriptions/personas, generates ratings as user responses to recommended items, and stores user-item interaction histories in a memory module.
categories.reviewer_notes: Planning and self-reflection modules are not reported.

categories.evidence: The paper trains RL recommender agents on SUBER for 1.6M steps using rewards generated by the simulated LLM environment.
categories.reviewer_notes: The simulator stores interaction history, but there is no explicit self-reflection or agent-to-agent feedback loop.

categories.evidence: User interaction history is updated after recommendations and used in later prompts; simulated rewards are used to train RL recommender models; observable interaction histories/features are updated by prior recommendations and responses.
categories.reviewer_notes: Individual preference updating is limited: the paper notes mostly static users, but interaction history and reward perturbation are used to represent changing/evolving preferences.

categories.evidence: RL recommenders are evaluated using average reward, MAP@10, MRR@10, personalization@10, and proportions of liked/disliked genres in recommendations.
categories.reviewer_notes: Personalization and liked/disliked genre alignment are coded as beyond-accuracy metrics. Scalability of recommender performance is not evaluated.

categories.evidence: The simulator is evaluated through ablation scores, comparison of simulated rating distributions to MovieLens ratings, and a human evaluation where participants rated LLM response quality.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper discusses model size and speed trade-offs but does not report a dedicated scalability evaluation.

result.paper_level_notes: Full text clearly meets the inclusion criteria. The paper introduces an LLM-based simulated user environment for RL recommender-system training and evaluation, with experiments in movie and book recommendation.

title: LLM-powered user simulator for recommender system
pdf_filename: LLM-Powered User Simulator for Recommender System.pdf

result.title: LLM-powered user simulator for recommender system
result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full paper explicitly proposes an LLM-powered user simulator for recommender-system simulation. The simulator uses LLMs to analyze item characteristics and user comments, produces simulated like/dislike user engagement, and is used to train/evaluate RL-based item recommendation algorithms across multiple datasets.
inclusion_criteria_triggered: Uses/proposes an LLM-powered simulated user/user response model
Used in recommender-system simulation for RL-based recommender training/evaluation
Involves item recommendation and simulated user engagement such as like/dislike responses

categories.evidence: Experiments use five datasets spanning Yelp, Amazon Music, Amazon Games, Amazon Movie, and Anime, described as POI, music, movie, game, and anime recommendation scenarios.
categories.reviewer_notes: Because the paper studies multiple recommendation domains, coded as general_purpose_recommender according to the schema.

categories.evidence: The paper discusses opacity, hallucination, privacy, computational cost, and simulator fidelity, but does not explicitly frame or address representation, measurement, historical, or evaluation bias.
categories.reviewer_notes: No explicit bias terminology or bias-mitigation objective was reported.

categories.evidence: The simulator combines logical models using if-then comparisons of positive/negative keyword matches and similarities, equations for αpos/αneg and βpos/βneg, random tie-breaking when scores are equal, and ML models including LLMs, BERT embeddings, and SASRec.
categories.reviewer_notes: Stochastic modelling is limited but supported by explicit rand{0,1} tie-breaking in the logical models.

categories.evidence: User modelling uses historical interactions h split into positive and negative item sets, ratings/comments from real datasets, and LLM-generated item preference keywords from objective item information and subjective user comments.
categories.reviewer_notes: The LLM primarily generates item pros/cons and sentiment keywords rather than full personas; coded llm_generated because these generated keywords are used to construct explicit user preference representations.

categories.evidence: The paper models user engagement through an explicit decision logic: users first identify what an item is and then assess how it aligns with past preferences and general comments.
categories.reviewer_notes: No personality theory or emotion/mood model is used. The cognition-inspired label is based on the stated decision-making logic rather than a formal cognitive theory.

categories.evidence: The simulator independently infers a user response yc such as like/dislike for a candidate item, and its response depends on the candidate item and the user's historical interactions h.
categories.reviewer_notes: No agent-to-agent social interaction or proactive behaviour such as deciding when to initiate/stop interaction is implemented; the simulator responds to recommendations.

categories.evidence: The simulator represents user preference through historical positive and negative item sets and keyword-based pros/cons, outputs user engagement actions such as like/dislike, and uses historical interactions h as past preference information.
categories.reviewer_notes: No planning or self-reflection module is described. Profile is coded as preference representation rather than demographic/persona profile.

categories.evidence: The simulator provides reward signals in an MDP formulation and is used to train reinforcement-learning recommender algorithms such as A2C, DQN, PPO, and TRPO.
categories.reviewer_notes: No self-reflection or agent-to-agent feedback loop is reported. The feedback loop is through recommender training using simulated interactions/rewards.

categories.evidence: The MDP state includes historical interactions and transitions to a new state after recommendations, while simulated rewards from the user simulator are used to train RL recommender models.
categories.reviewer_notes: The ML feedback loop is clear. The individual feedback loop is coded conservatively because the paper formulates sequential state transitions with history, but does not emphasize preference updating through self-reflection.

categories.evidence: The paper evaluates RL recommendation algorithms with average reward, total reward, and liking ratio in top-10 recommendations across datasets.
categories.reviewer_notes: No diversity, novelty, fairness, or other beyond-accuracy metric is reported for recommender evaluation. Runtime is reported for simulator comparison, not recommender evaluation.

categories.evidence: The simulator is compared with SUBER and KuaiSim using A.Rwd, T.Rwd, AUC, and inference time, and experiments are conducted on public offline datasets including Yelp, Amazon, and Anime ratings/comments.
categories.reviewer_notes: No live user testing or online experiment with real users is reported.

result.paper_level_notes: The simulator uses the LLM offline to generate item/user-sentiment keyword descriptions, then combines logical keyword/similarity models with a pretrained SASRec statistical model to simulate binary like/dislike responses for RL-based recommender-system training.

categories.reviewer_notes: The human comparison comes from real production A/B traffic, likely analysed as logged outcomes; coded as both offline logs and real-world user testing/online experiment evidence.

title: AgentGR: Semantic-aware Agentic Group Decision-Making Simulator for Group Recommendation
pdf_filename: AgentGR Semantic-aware Agentic Group Decision-Making Simulator for Group Recommendation.pdf

result.title: AgentGR: Semantic-aware Agentic Group Decision-Making Simulator for Group Recommendation
result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full text proposes AgentGR, an LLM-driven multi-agent simulator for group recommendation. It constructs user preference profiles from interaction logs and textual item descriptions, uses user agents for member role-playing, and simulates group decision-making through static and dynamic multi-agent strategies for top-k item recommendation.
inclusion_criteria_triggered: Uses LLM-driven agents as simulated user/member agents for role-playing and group decision-making simulation
Used in a recommender-system simulation context: group recommendation
Evaluates item recommendation with top-k metrics such as HR@K and NDCG@K

categories.evidence: Experiments use MafengwoS from a tourism website for group travel activities and Weeplaces, a check-in dataset for group gathering activities in restaurants/locations.
categories.reviewer_notes: Domain is best described as travel/POI/group activity recommendation, which is outside the listed specific domains.

categories.evidence: The paper focuses on group recommendation accuracy, semantic preference profiling, leadership, and group decision simulation; it does not explicitly address bias as a research objective.
categories.reviewer_notes: A baseline is described as addressing preference bias, but AgentGR itself does not explicitly study bias.

categories.evidence: The system uses GPT-4o/LLMs for preference extraction, user agents, ranking, and group discussion; the static strategy follows a predefined two-stage workflow; equations define meta-path construction, preference functions, and leader selection via cosine similarity.
categories.reviewer_notes: Symbolic equations mainly support profile construction and leadership recognition rather than being the sole user-behaviour model.

categories.evidence: User profiles are constructed from user-item interactions, group-item interactions, group-user affiliations, and textual descriptions of previously interacted items; LLMs are prompted to extract, integrate, and refine user preference profiles.
categories.reviewer_notes: No evidence that user attributes are randomly sampled.

categories.evidence: The paper frames group decision-making as involving preference expression, compromise, and consensus-building, and describes Chain-of-Preference reasoning as mimicking human inductive and reflective reasoning.
categories.reviewer_notes: No personality traits or affect/emotion modelling are reported.

categories.evidence: User agents individually rank candidate items based on their preference profiles and group topics; the dynamic strategy lets user agents engage in multi-round discussions guided by group topic and leader; group consensus is judged before ending or continuing discussion.
categories.reviewer_notes: Proactiveness is not coded because agents do not decide when to initiate interaction or leave; they operate within assigned recommendation workflows.

categories.evidence: AgentGR creates refined user preference profiles; user agents rank candidate items and express preferences in discussions; profiles are derived from historical user/group interactions and item descriptions.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper includes a 're-thinking preference refinement' step, but it is profile distillation rather than an ongoing self-reflection module updating behaviour over interactions.

categories.evidence: In the dynamic strategy, user agents conduct multi-round discussions, a group agent summarizes, and a judgment agent evaluates consensus; if consensus is not reached, additional discussion rounds begin.
categories.reviewer_notes: No recommender retraining or longitudinal user-state update loop is reported.

categories.evidence: The dynamic simulation uses consensus judgment outcomes to determine whether the simulated group decision process concludes or continues with more discussion rounds.
categories.reviewer_notes: This is a within-decision feedback loop, not a longitudinal recommender-user feedback loop; no ML-model, sampling, or individual preference-update feedback loop is reported.

categories.evidence: Recommendation performance is evaluated with HR@K and NDCG@K on MafengwoS and Weeplaces. The paper also compares inference time and token costs for static versus dynamic simulation strategies and discusses LLM scale/type cost trade-offs.
categories.reviewer_notes: No diversity, novelty, fairness, or other beyond-accuracy recommender metrics are reported.

categories.evidence: The group decision simulation is evaluated through recommendation accuracy on real datasets using held-out interactions, static/dynamic strategy comparison, user-profile quality analysis with GPT-4o and human annotators, and time/token cost analysis.
categories.reviewer_notes: Human annotators evaluate profile quality, but the paper does not report live user testing or online experiments with actual recommender users.

result.paper_level_notes: The paper is relevant because it explicitly uses LLM-driven user agents for group recommendation simulation. It also uses LLMs for recommendation/ranking, but this is coupled with simulated user/member agents and group decision-making rather than being only an LLM recommender.

result.full_text_reasoning_brief: The full text confirms the paper proposes an LLM-based simulated user agent for conversational recommender systems and sales-agent dialogue evaluation. This triggers the exclusion criterion for conversational recommender systems where the LLM is mainly used in a dialogue setting.

inclusion_criteria_triggered: Uses/proposes/evaluates an LLM-based simulated user agent or user response model

The setting involves item recommendation/purchase decisions over recommended products

categories.evidence: The experiments use Amazon Reviews 2023 domains, specifically Electronics and Video Games, and model shopping scenarios, sales agents, budgets, and purchase decisions.
categories.reviewer_notes: Although two product domains are used, both are Amazon product-shopping settings, so e_commerce is the best fit.

categories.evidence: The paper states that existing LLM-based simulators produce unrealistically high acceptance rates, which can inflate estimates of CRS performance and obscure intention–behavior frictions.

categories.reviewer_notes: All selected techniques are explicitly described in the Decision Module and Response Module.

categories.evidence: User profiles are synthesized from Amazon Reviews 2023; openness and weights are derived from historical reviews, and budget is sampled from the interquartile range of prices within a category.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper uses LLM-based analysis for some inferred traits, but it does not clearly state that LLMs generate full personas or profiles, so llm_generated is not selected.

categories.evidence: The framework explicitly models human decision-making under choice overload, cognitive constraints, heuristic-to-compensatory item evaluation, and decision deferral; personas include traits such as openness, pickiness, and preference uncertainty.
categories.reviewer_notes: The strongest basis is cognitive/decision-theoretic. Personality-aware is selected because explicit persona traits are modeled, although the paper does not deeply ground them in a named personality theory.

categories.evidence: The User Agent independently generates responses, evaluates sales responses using global state and dialogue history, interacts turn-by-turn with a Sales Agent, initializes the dialogue with needs, and can choose communicative actions such as accept, reject, ask follow-up, request clarification, or defer.
categories.reviewer_notes: Proactiveness is coded because the user agent can initiate the interaction and select actions beyond passive acceptance; however, most interaction is still turn-based.

categories.evidence: The system defines a global user state with persona and scenario; maintains dialogue history H; includes action selection and response synthesis; and has specialized Decision, Selection, and Hesitation Modules.
categories.reviewer_notes: Planning and self-reflection are not selected because the paper does not describe multi-step planning or reflective preference updates.

categories.evidence: The simulation is a turn-based dialogue between a Sales Agent and User Agent, with dialogue history updated after each sales response and user response until purchase or the turn limit.
categories.reviewer_notes: No retraining or self-reflective updating is implemented. Coding is limited to the conversational feedback arising from agent-to-agent interaction.

categories.evidence: Sales-agent recommendations lead to user outcomes such as accept, reject, or defer, and the dialogue history is updated with these outcomes for subsequent turns.
categories.reviewer_notes: This is a weak conversational feedback loop only. The paper does not model recommender retraining, population sampling feedback, or explicit preference updating.

categories.evidence: The experiments primarily evaluate user-agent/simulator behavior and conversational simulation quality, not the recommender algorithm itself; the sales agent is used as a fixed interaction partner.
categories.reviewer_notes: Success rate could be used for CRS/sales-agent evaluation in principle, but in this paper it is mainly reported to compare user simulators and decision modules.

categories.evidence: The simulator is evaluated with success rate, subjective dialogue quality, believability/hallucination ratio, overload-sensitivity experiments, psychological-economics reproduction tests, and ablations.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper uses Amazon review data to construct scenarios, but does not compare simulated behavior against offline user logs or live user-testing results.

result.paper_level_notes: Excluded at full-text stage because the setting is explicitly conversational recommender systems with LLM-based user dialogue simulation, which matches the specified CRS exclusion criterion. Coding is still provided for available simulator details.

categories.reviewer_notes: Domain is scholarly/scientific paper recommendation, which is outside the listed movie/news/music/e-commerce categories.

categories.evidence: The benchmark freezes candidate pools and temporal boundaries to avoid incomparable evaluation from dynamic crawling, data updates, and future-information leakage; Appendix A.4 says fixed pools avoid data bias introduced by dynamic crawling or real-time retrieval.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper does not mainly frame this as fairness/bias work. Coded evaluation_bias only because evaluation leakage/data-bias concerns are explicitly discussed.

categories.evidence: User selections are simulated based on oracle labels, system rank, system label, and drift-topic matches. The paper defines scoring/update equations and drift functions, and Appendix C.3 reports stochastic drift settings such as drift_probability = 0.5.
categories.reviewer_notes: These techniques apply to the paper's non-LLM simulated users/profile dynamics. The LLM is not used as the simulated user response model, so machine_learning_model is not selected for user simulation.

categories.evidence: Cold-start profile construction uses an LLM to extract and canonicalize directions, methods, application contexts, authors, institutions, and preference clues into fixed profile fields; prompts parse user descriptions into structured profile-update signals.
categories.reviewer_notes: The benchmark's 24 simulated researcher profiles are described as reproducible simulated profiles, but their exact construction basis is not fully reported. Label reflects LLM-supported profile construction in the method, not LLM-based user-agent simulation.

categories.evidence: The paper models interests, short-term reading signals, and interest drift, but does not report a psychological theory, personality construct, affect model, or explicit cognitive model for simulated users.
categories.reviewer_notes: Interest drift is behavioral/state modelling; conservatively not coded as cognition_inspired because no psychological basis is specified.

categories.evidence: The simulator records selected papers after Top-20 recommendations, and profile/drift state is updated across days from selections, skips, reading requests, and feedback signals.
categories.reviewer_notes: Capabilities refer to the non-LLM simulated user/profile loop. There is no LLM-based user agent; no social_ability or proactiveness is reported.

categories.evidence: The framework maintains structured scholarly profiles, simulates selected papers/reading actions, stores historical feedback and reading-signal state, and includes a drift-adaptation state/module.
categories.reviewer_notes: Other refers to the explicit drift-adaptation state. No planning module or clear self-reflection module for an LLM user agent is reported.

categories.evidence: The daily loop updates user state from feedback: selections, corrections, sustained reading, skips, reading requests, report feedback, and profile edits are folded into next-day profiles and drift state.
categories.reviewer_notes: The paper implements feedback-driven profile/drift updating, but not an LLM user agent reflecting in natural language. Coded as self_reflection because this is the closest available label for preference/state updates from prior interactions.

categories.evidence: Each simulated user's profile and drift state are updated over consecutive daily recommendation episodes based on that user's selections and feedback history.
categories.reviewer_notes: No retraining of the recommender/user model with simulated data, agent-population sampling loop, or agent-to-agent feedback loop is reported.

categories.evidence: The paper reports gNDCG@20, Useful@5/@20, OracleRecall@20, MRR@20, SelectedNDCG@20, RecommendationScore, HumanEval, drift adaptation metrics, real-user satisfaction, and token-cost/scale statistics across 1,200 episodes and LLM backbones.
categories.reviewer_notes: Beyond-accuracy is coded for behavioral alignment, human usefulness, satisfaction, report usefulness, and drift-adaptation evaluation; scalability is coded for token cost and benchmark-scale reporting.

categories.evidence: The paper states simulated relevance labels are not human ground truth and the real-user pilot is a user-experience sanity check. Human evaluation validates recommendation metrics/expert judgments rather than directly evaluating simulator fidelity against logs or live-user behavior.
categories.reviewer_notes: Although the paper uses simulated users and includes human evaluation and a real-user pilot, it does not clearly evaluate the user simulator or compare simulated user responses against real logs/users.

result.paper_level_notes: Excluded for the target review because the full paper does not use an LLM as a simulated user agent/user response model. It remains relevant as a scientific-paper recommender benchmark with simulated user-day episodes and feedback loops, but the LLM functions are system-side profile parsing, explanation, and report generation.
